From the team behind Notting Hill’s acclaimed Dorian and Eel Sushi comes the grand Nakimushi, which will feature a ground-floor ramen bar and a more refined 25-seater upstairs restaurant serving a broader spectrum of Japanese cuisine. Chefs Yuji Shimokawa Kelly and Robin Kosuge gave both concepts successful trial runs at their Urchin and Robin's Ramen residencies at Holland Park’s Supermarket of Dreams, so expect a giddy and receptive audience as well as a busy signal when trying to book a table.
Opens: September 7
Address: 7 Kensington Mall, London, W8 4EB
6. The very posh pub
The Horses, Clerkenwell
With west London’s Fat Badger, Pelican and Hero as well as the Bull in Charlbury, Public House Group have finessed the art of the modern gastropub; putty-coloured plaster walls, artsy foxed mirrors and buffed wood finishes. Oh and extremely good cooking. The Horses is their first move east, and will bring their seasonal, Cotswolds-grown produce to the table. After something fishy? There’ll also be a host of seafood here at this former site of the 1897-built Coach & Horses.
Opens: Late September
Address: 26-28 Ray Street, Clerkenwell, EC1R 5ER
![Macbeth x Hot Fresh Pizza](https://media.timeout.com/images/106440801/image.webp) 
7. The Portuguese pizza spesh
The Macbeth x Fresh Hot Pizza at The Fox, Haggerston
What’s a monthly London restaurant update without a little pizza news, eh? This isn’t a new parlour but rather a week-long pop-up that brings together two local heroes; the revamped Macbeth’s Portuguese kitchen and the team behind Fresh Hot Pizza at the also newly revamped Fox. What happens when you bring them together? A pizza that pays tribute to Porto’s wet and wild Francesinha sandwich, dripping with mozzarella, and with sausage, ground beef and pork belly bobbing about like islands in the stream of cheese.
Available: August 31 to September 6
Address: 372 Kingsland Road, Haggerston, E8 4DA
![InterStellar BBQ](https://media.timeout.com/images/106436078/image.webp) 
8. The Michelin star BBQ takeover
InterStellar BBQ x La Barbecue at The Ned, City
American meat institutions InterStellar BBQ and La Barbecue are coming to London for a serious BBQ collaboration. Two of the best little smokehouses in Texas, these Michelin-recommended Austin spots are popping up at The Ned for a one-month residency, with pitmasters John Bates and Ali Clem prepping the ‘ultimate BBQ tray’, featuring peach tea glazed pork belly, pulled lamb shoulder, chimichurri beef short rib, pork ribs and chopped cheese sausage. Unbuckle your belts now in preparation.
Available: September 4 - October 4
Address: Electric Bar & Diner, The Ned, 27 Poultry, City, EC2R 8AJ
![Seouls of Mischief](https://media.timeout.com/images/106440804/image.webp) 
9. The punchy pub kitchen
Seouls of Mischief at The Adam & Eve, Homerton
Mexican-Korean fusion street food folk Mexican Seoul are giving their burger-based off-shoot Seouls of Mischief a spin at east London boozer, the Adam & Eve. Come for the smash burgers and wings as well as the elote corn ribs and stay for the weird ‘L’ shaped pool table. But try not to drink so many pints that you have to call ‘daddy come and get me’.
Launches: September 4
Address: 155 Homerton High Street, E9 6AS
![Beefbar](https://media.timeout.com/images/106440805/image.webp) 
10. The flash hotel resto revamp
Beefbar at Broadwick Soho, Soho
Broadwick Soho’s in-house restaurant is starting over again and ditching their Dear Jackie basement restaurant and replacing it with a branch of glitzy global brand Beefbar. The Chelsea outpost, Le Petit Beefbar, closed earlier this year in preparation. Expect this to be as razzle-dazzle as the Monte Carlo, Paris, Mykonos and New York outposts, with Japanese Kobe and Australian Wagyu served in an outré room, where everything’s beautiful in its own way.
Opens: September 14
Address: 20 Broadwick Street, Soho, W1F 8HT
![Pizzas on the menu at Five Feet](https://media.timeout.com/images/106432267/image.webp) 
11. Pan pizza perfection
Five Feet, Bermondsey
More pizza news! Five Feet Pizza comes from three heavyweights of the London food scene: Jay Patel (co-founder of Legare and Luna), Roland Horne (founder and CEO of WatchHouse) and Jack Ellingham (former chef and baker at Dusty Knuckle). They’ll be serving pan pizzas with spongy centimetre-thick dough (not quite thick enough to qualify as deep-dish). So powerful it might make your false eyelashes fall off.
Opens: September
Address: 4 Tanner Street, Bermondsey, SE1 3LE
![Duda Diner](https://media.timeout.com/images/106440806/image.webp) 
12. Malaysian magic in west London
Duda Diner at The Pilgrim, Paddington
After coming to the end of their Nunhead residency, Hakeem and Zura Ahmad of Duda Diner bring their superior nasi lemak and kerabu salad to The Pilgrim as the final part of the hotel’s 2026 Incubator Kitchen Series. Ideal for date night with your potential new boy (or girl) friend.
Available: September 17 to late December
Address: 25 London Street, Paddington, W2 1HH
![DUMBO burger](https://media.timeout.com/images/106431601/image.webp) 
13. Serious smash burgers for Soho
Dumbo, Soho
Dumbo’s second London burger joint will serve the same sleek cheeseburgers and fries as their Bethnal Green Road location. The French-born brand’s double patty smash burgers are bulked out with gleaming American cheese as well as plump pickles and ketchup and mustard. Dumbo also offers a vegetarian ‘Earth burger’ option, as well as fries and nuggets. If you eat like a little bird, this one ain’t for you.
Opens: September 4
Address: 37 Berwick Street, Soho, W1F 8RS
![Avinash Shashidhara/Talli Queen](https://media.timeout.com/images/106440811/image.webp) 
14. An Indian gastro-boozer
Talli Queen, Shepherd’s Bush
Former River Café cook and Pahli Hill head chef Avinash Shashidhara is opening a slick desi gastropub on the site of what was the Queen Adelaide pub. The menu will include ‘Military canteen-style meatballs’, chicken and liver pepper fry, Kerala chilli beef and Bangalore-inspired dosa. There’ll be roasts every Sunday, with slow-cooked lamb shoulder and biryani to share. With a great bar, there’ll be no reason to hurry home.
Opens: September
Address: 412 Uxbridge Road, W12 0NR.
![Rack City Ribs](https://media.timeout.com/images/106440813/image.webp) 
15. Soul food BBQ
Rack City Ribs at Kitchen E20, Stratford
Something’s burning? Nope, it’s just the excellent Rack City Ribs, previously in residence at north London honky tonk the Dukes of Highgate. They’re now swinging over to Kitchen E20 at the Stratford Hotel for a three month pop-up. Expect Caribbean-edged barbecue, with crispy jerk pork ribs, battered boar sausage and chicken wings with pineapple glaze.
Launches: September 1
Address: The Stratford Hotel, 20 International Way, London E20 1GQ
Get the latest and greatest from the Big Smoke – from news and reviews to events and trends. Just follow our Time Out London WhatsApp channel.
Stay in the loop: sign up to our free Time Out London newsletter for the best of the city, straight to your inbox.
summary: London's restaurant scene is experiencing a major autumn surge with 15 notable openings, residencies, and pop-ups launching in September 2026. The lineup features high-profile collaborations, new ventures from celebrated chefs, and diverse culinary styles ranging from Turkish meze and French bistros to Texas barbecue and pan pizzas. These establishments span across various neighborhoods, bringing fresh dining concepts to central and outer London alike.
key_points: Chef Sertaç Dirik and David Carter are opening a Turkish restaurant named Kid in Soho.
Public House Group is expanding eastward with the opening of a modern gastropub called The Horses in Clerkenwell.
Bunso in Kentish Town introduces a unique concept that operates as a Filipino bakery during the day and a pizza joint at night.
Several high-profile pop-ups and residencies launch in September, including Texas smokehouses InterStellar BBQ and La Barbecue at The Ned.
Dumbo is opening its second London burger joint in Soho, serving its signature French-born double patty smash burgers.

title: Why London's ground will be slow to recover from the drought
author: Briohny Williams
content:
![Aerial view of a church surrounded by drought-hit grassland, with central London visible in the distance](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/2372/live/3e95c1c0-9fa8-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
All Saints church, Blackheath, surrounded by drought-hit grassland
- Published
London is still experiencing drought conditions and, despite recent rain, much of the capital's ground will take time to recover after weeks of record-breaking dry weather.
About 80% of London sits on clay, which extends to depths of more than 100m (328ft) in some places.
The clay has lost moisture, causing it to shrink and crack. In some cases, this can lead to subsidence, resulting in damage to buildings and homes.
Sustained rainfall over a prolonged period will be needed for the ground to fully recover, experts say. Rob Higginson, a geotechnical engineer, says it will be a "very slow process" and that "a single downpour is not going to do it".
![Aerial view of dry, yellow grassland in a London park, with the city skyline in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/f124/live/388246a0-9fa8-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Parks and green areas across London have dried out owing to the hot weather
July was the driest on record for England and Wales, and a hosepipe ban remains in place for Thames Water and Affinity Water customers in London following prolonged dry weather, low rainfall and increased demand for water.
Higginson said that while "putting a hose on the ground will keep your grass growing, it won't affect the underlying clay at all".
He explained how recent heatwaves had affected clay deep underground.
"If the clay gets warm, it loses volume, and it's going to go down and contract.
"You get the cracking, but you also get downward movement. If a house is sitting on top of the clay, it will go down with it."
He said this predominantly affects homes built between the post-war period and the 1980s.
![Rob Higginson standing in a dry London park where grass has turned brown during drought conditions.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/e913/live/71d124d0-9fa8-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Rob Higginson, a geotechnical engineer, says London's clay ground needs prolonged rain
However, even when rain does arrive, he said the recovery process would not be straightforward.
Higginson said: "The topsoil will absorb a certain amount of it, and then it will go down and sit on the clay layer.
"Then you've got surface runoff, so the excess water will just run off.
"What you really need is prolonged rain. It doesn't have to be intense, just a reasonable amount over a long period of time, so it has time to percolate into the very fine voids in the London clay."
Even when the grass begins to turn green again, the clay beneath may take much longer to recover from the effects of this summer's drought.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: London remains in drought conditions following record-breaking dry weather, and the capital's predominantly clay ground will take a long time to recover. The loss of moisture has caused the clay to shrink, crack, and potentially lead to subsidence that can damage homes. Experts state that a single downpour or surface watering will not fix the issue, and that sustained, prolonged rainfall is necessary for the ground to fully recover.
key_points: About 80% of London sits on clay that has lost moisture, shrunk, and cracked due to record-breaking dry weather and heatwaves.
The ground shrinkage can cause subsidence and downward movement, potentially damaging buildings and homes built between the post-war period and the 1980s.
A hosepipe ban remains in place for Thames Water and Affinity Water customers in London following low rainfall and increased water demand.
Geotechnical engineer Rob Higginson explains that recovering the deep clay layer requires prolonged rain over a long period so water can percolate into the fine voids.

title: Notting Hill Carnival 2026: Parade in full flow on 60th anniversary - live updates
author: Niva Yadav; Matt Watts
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/30/12/01M1948GXQCD05CD7EK071BARG.jpg?trim=0,0,670,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
The annual celebration of Caribbean culture will see mas bands, steel pan bands, dancers, and sound systems light up the west London district in colour, glitter, and feathers.
Following Saturday’s Steel Band Competition, today sees the colourful J’ouvert opening celebration at Ladbroke Grove followed by the much-anticipated Children’s Day and Dutty Mas parade, kicking off at Westbourne Park.
Stay with us as we bring you the latest from the carnival weekend.
Scroll down for the latest updates.
Live updates
Heavy police presence to keep crowds and masqueraders safe
There is a heavy police presence in W10, with as many as 7,000 officers across the district for carnival this bank holiday weekend.
The Met will endeavour to keep crowds safe, while stewards will help to redirect spectators. There could be as many as two million revellers joining in on festivities across today and tomorrow.
Mas bands also are required to have their own security to keep them safe along the police route.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/30/11/03/6a21b495-2016-4578-a1ff-45bb5a6fd80f.JPG?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640)
Crowds join in the celebrations
Spectators are all joining in on the festivities, with crowds bopping up and down as the Children’s Day parade gets into full swing.
The Standard’s Luke Reevey says the atmosphere “is electric” with the children receiving the loudest applause from the crowds.
“It’s like one big dance floor!”
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/30/11/37/27599b4c-dd81-4e31-b93a-0bfcfe3eaefa.JPG?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640)
Notting Hill Carnival embraces next generation
Children’s Day is really about passing the baton onto the next generation. Dozens of family mas bands will feature children dressed in elaborate costumes, celebrating the history of their ancestors.
![Notting Hill Carnival 2026: Children's Parade celebrates next generation of revellers](https://cdn.ex.co/transformations-account/production/761715bb-261d-4032-af09-a493a82bd926/7649ee5c-edfe-4a5e-8df0-b3e566628c01/thumbnail-360.webp)
'Huge endeavour', says Sir Sadiq Khan
Sir Sadiq Khan has called hosting one of the world’s biggest street festivals “a huge endeavour” as he thanked the organisers, volunteers, and emergency services for their efforts at Notting Hill Carnival.
Electric vibes as procession gets going
The vibes at Notting Hill Carnival are electric as the procession gets moving down the parade route.
A slight delay saw bands stranded on Great Western Road as they waited for the opening ceremony, but Europe’s largest street party is now away!
The sounds of calypso, drumming, steel pans, and soca can be heard as crowds cheer on the masqueraders.
![Notting Hill Carnival: Electric vibes as masqueraders and carnival-goers get the party started](https://cdn.ex.co/transformations-account/production/761715bb-261d-4032-af09-a493a82bd926/ca444a12-85c6-4f97-a9bd-69e30c4a0bf8/thumbnail-360.webp)
What happens at the opening ceremony?
The parade is underway, but first there will be a short speech by organisers to officially mark the start of carnival.
Former chairman of Notting Hill Carnival Ansel Wong has taken to the mic as the festivities get underway on Great Western Road. Stood beside him is the current chair, Ian Comfort.
He paid tribute to the carnival’s history, while also congratulating the successes of Carnival thus far as an “English icon”.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/30/10/43/Ansel-Wong-at-Notting-Hill-Carnival.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640)
What is playing mas?
You don’t “do mas”, you play mas! Playing mas means to participate in the carnival festivities by wearing a costume, dancing, and making noise as you parade around Notting Hill.
It’s about bringing your costume to life and putting on a show for spectators as you showcase Caribbean culture on the road.
![Notting Hill Carnival 2026: Revellers play mas as carnival gets underway](https://cdn.ex.co/transformations-account/production/761715bb-261d-4032-af09-a493a82bd926/d29c7941-151e-4d7b-8d19-bb11db352e22/thumbnail-360.webp)
Spectators travel from across the UK for Notting Hill Carnival 2026
Spectators have travelled from across the UK to celebrate Notting Hill Carnival this morning.
Blue, in her sixties, has travelled from Blackpool for the celebrations. She said she’s been waiting as long as 30 years to come down to W10 for Europe’s largest street festival.
She said: “Finally, the schedule’s opened up to allow me to come down. [I’m looking forward to] the colours and the costumes, because they’re quite spectacular.”
Blue added that the atmosphere at the opening of the parade was “energetic”, “bubbly”, and “amazing.”
What is jab jab?
Carnival masquerade is deeply rooted in African traditions and evolved to create satirical characters following enslavement in the Caribbean.
Jab Jab is just one character you’ll see on the streets of W10, derived from the French patois word for devil, “diable”.
Slave owners often used the word devil as a derogatory label for enslaved Africans. But this was later reclaimed to mock the planter classes.
Jab Jab dress includes covering skin in black oil as a symbol of resistance against racism and wearing horns or chains.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/30/10/38/b96cd986-c045-4d2d-a106-f778ad3a9492.JPG?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640)
Why are some people wearing T-shirts?
The eagle-eyed among you will have noticed that not all masqueraders are wearing full-costume. Many will be wearing t-shirts as they make their way around the parade route.
Branded t-shirts are popular ways of getting involved in a mas band without having to fork out for a costume, while others simply prefer to be comfortable. Dutty mas bands in particular will only wear t-shirts or leotards as they throw paints and colour at each other. But, regulations mean that only a third of masqueraders per band are allowed to wear t-shirts. The rest must be in costume.
There’s a whole variety of costume options, from full frontline outfits to bikini mas and backpacks with all the bells and whistles. The options are endless!
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/30/11/01M1917MB39EWPMWAVDH4ZCFZF.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640)
summary: The 60th anniversary of the Notting Hill Carnival is underway in west London, featuring the J'ouvert opening celebration and Children's Day parade. The annual celebration of Caribbean culture has drawn up to two million revellers and features a heavy police presence of around 7,000 officers. Despite a brief opening delay, crowds are enjoying the electric atmosphere, music, and elaborate costumes.
key_points: Up to 7,000 police officers are deployed across the district to keep crowds and masqueraders safe during the bank holiday weekend.
Children's Day highlights family mas bands and passes the baton of Caribbean culture to the next generation.
Sir Sadiq Khan praised the festival as a huge endeavour and thanked organisers, volunteers, and emergency services.
The event features traditional elements like Jab Jab alongside various costume options, including branded t-shirts and full frontline outfits.

title: Influencer sobs in court as he denies robbing man of designer watch in central London
author: Shaun Wilson
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/29/15/01M0ZDX985MNT40ATQZTQSF1X0.jpg?trim=0,208,0,208&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
An influencer broke down in tears in court as he denied helping to rob a fashion designer of his diamond-encrusted watch in central London.
Abdel El Habchi, 30, who has around a million followers on Facebook, and Ali Eldahouzze, 22, are accused of robbing designer Catalin Botezatu. Jurors were told a third man, Younes Djoudi, has pleaded guilty to robbery.
Mr Botezatu, who is a Romanian entrepreneur, had been having dinner with his assistant and a friend before he was allegedly robbed of his Richard Mille watch worth more than £137,000 by the trio, Southwark Crown Court heard.
Giving evidence on Friday, El Habchi told jurors through an Arabic interpreter: “I had no idea it was going to happen, I did not participate, I didn’t know even that a watch was snatched or stolen until later on.”
Read More
The court heard Mr Botezatu had been smoking a cigar with a friend on the terrace of Latin American restaurant Amazonico in Berkeley Square on the evening of January 28.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/29/15/01M0X95SS4JQQ1QKJ141NN4K49.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Prosecutors allege that the watch was later cut from his wrist shortly before midnight.
El Habchi, who grew up in a town near Casablanca, Morocco, told the court he came to the UK in 2019 on a spouse visa and is married with two children.
Jurors heard that El Habchi had been working as a security guard, but also has a Facebook following of around a million, around 350,000 Instagram followers and a TikTok account.
The defendant said he and his friend, Eldahouzze, had been travelling from Slough to Soho, central London, hours before the alleged robbery when Eldahouzze received a call from Djoudi telling him to meet in Mayfair.
El Habchi told jurors that while in Djoudi’s car close to the restaurant, he sat in the back watching TikTok videos and heard Djoudi being “threatening” and aggressive towards Eldahouzze.
While walking around the area later on, he saw Djoudi “use his hand to grab something from the hand” of a man, the court heard.
Explaining why he ran from the scene, El Habchi said: “At that moment it was panic and after one or two seconds when I see Ali run I was panicked and I was completely lost, I had never been in this situation before.”
El Habchi said that Eldahouzze later told him that Djoudi had threatened him to “execute what he asked him to do”.
Asked by his barrister, Loheswaran Amirthananthar, how he felt at the time, El Habchi replied: “To be honest with you I felt as if I was betrayed, I had no idea what was happening and I found myself in this problem.”
He said Eldahouzze told him he was “scared” of Djoudi.
El Habchi told jurors that Djoudi met the pair the following morning with the watch.
Asked whether any threats had been made against him, El Habchi tearfully replied: “He turned to me and made a threat ‘if you report anything to the police I will burn your kids’.”
He said he was “under threat” and “scared” of Djoudi, who he claimed “has a lot of connections”.
He added: “I was just concentrating on my kids’ safety. I was really scared and I find myself in the middle of a deep problem.”
The court heard that all three men were incarcerated at Wandsworth prison after their arrests.
El Habchi said that in April he was attacked by around 16 people in the prison and that Djoudi had “instigated” the assault.
He told jurors he suffered a cut to his back and was stamped on the head.
Prosecutor Arizuna Asante told the court on Tuesday that after leaving the restaurant, Mr Botezatu “stood near the car smoking for a few minutes with his friend before he was approached by three males”.
Mr Asante told jurors: “The three males surrounded Mr Botezatu and robbed him of his watch by wresting it from his left wrist.
“It is believed a knife was used to cut through the rubber strap because the victim had cuts on his wrists after the watch was taken.”
Mr Asante, cross-examining El Habchi on Friday afternoon, said: “I’m going to suggest to you Mr El Habchi, that your intention in going to Berkeley Square was to see if there was anybody there with a high-value watch to steal or rob from them?”
The defendant replied: “No.”
The prosecutor added: “That’s why, isn’t it, that you, Mr Djoudi and Mr Eldahouzze walked up and down Amazonico eyeing Mr Botezatu as a target?”
El Habchi replied: “I have no idea about this no.”
Prosecutors say the watch would now be worth “significantly more” than 160,000 euro.
El Habchi and Eldahouzze each deny one count of robbery.
The trial continues.
summary: Social media influencer Abdel El Habchi broke down in tears in court while denying involvement in the robbery of a diamond-encrusted Richard Mille watch from fashion designer Catalin Botezatu in central London. El Habchi and co-defendant Ali Eldahouzze both deny one count of robbery, while a third man, Younes Djoudi, has already pleaded guilty. El Habchi testified that he had no idea a robbery was going to happen, claimed he panicked at the scene, and stated he was later threatened by Djoudi regarding the safety of his children.
key_points: Abdel El Habchi and Ali Eldahouzze are on trial at Southwark Crown Court denying a robbery charge, while Younes Djoudi has pleaded guilty.
Fashion designer Catalin Botezatu was allegedly robbed of a watch worth more than £137,000 outside a restaurant in Berkeley Square.
Prosecutors allege the victim's watch was cut from his wrist using a knife.
El Habchi testified that he was unaware of the plot, panicked during the incident, and stayed silent because Djoudi threatened to harm his children.
The trial remains ongoing.

title: Ulez expansion three years on: How London's pollution gap persists
author: Annika Grosser
content:
![A blue road sign reading "Ultra low emission ZONE ULEZ Â½ mile ahead" beside a busy, tree-lined London road with cars and pedestrians.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/19ae/live/ece13af0-94d3-11f1-b2ab-0dd01740f9f6.jpg)
London's Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan introduced the Ultra-Low Emission Zone (Ulez) in central London in 2019 to improve air quality by taxing polluting vehicles
- Published
When her nine-year-old daughter died of an asthma attack in 2013, Rosamund Adoo-Kissi-Debrah had never heard about air pollution being a possible trigger for asthma.
After a medical report suggested a direct link between Ella's illness and illegal air pollution levels near her home, an inquest into her death was opened. Ella became the first person in the UK to have air pollution listed on her death certificate.
The coroner recorded that "there was a recognised failure to reduce the level of nitrogen dioxide to within the limits set by EU and domestic law".
A spokesperson from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) told the BBC that the government was committed to reducing air pollution, which "robs people of their health and costs the NHS millions of pounds every year".
Ella grew up in Lewisham in south-east London, near the South Circular Road, where her family still lives today. Although her mother said things had improved, she said more work was needed.
"The first steps of cleaning up the air in London with Ulez (Ultra Low Emission Zone) have clearly been worth it," Adoo-Kissi-Debrah said. "There is still so much more to do."
![Rosamund Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, wearing a pale blue three-piece suit and sunglasses, stands outside the High Court in London. The large Victorian Gothic Revival-style stone building with the 'Royal Courts of Justice' crest is visible in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/98f5/live/b1ff0b30-94d6-11f1-b2ab-0dd01740f9f6.jpg)
Rosamund Adoo-Kissi-Debrah outside the High Court following a hearing in July 2024
New BBC analysis shows London's air has improved substantially over the past decade. Average nitrogen dioxide (NOâ) levels have fallen by almost 38% since 2014 and every neighbourhood now meets the UK's legal limit, an annual average of 40 micrograms per cubic meter (Î¼ g/mÂ³).
But fewer than 1% of neighbourhoods meet the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommended guideline. At 10 Î¼ g/mÂ³, it is a quarter of the UK's legal limit.
More deprived areas and neighbourhoods with larger non-white populations saw some of the biggest reductions in air pollution over the decade. But they also started with much higher levels of NOâ and remain among the most polluted parts of London.
"We don't all breathe the same air," said Adoo-Kissi-Debrah.
The BBC's analysis used modelled air pollution data produced by Defra, together with census ethnicity data and income deprivation data from the UK government's Index of Multiple Deprivation.
After Ella's death, before the inquest, Sir Stephen Holgate, professor of immunopharmacology at the University of Southampton, examined her medical papers. He concluded that high levels of air pollution in Ella's neighbourhood contributed to the severity of her asthma and, ultimately, her death.
"Air pollution is always talked about as an environmental issue. It's not talked about as a health issue," he said.
Speaking recently to the BBC, Holgate argued reducing pollution was essential, but added that unless the government also tackled interconnected issues like poverty, housing, overcrowding and health inequalities, the burden of air pollution would continue to fall unequally.
The WHO states air pollution can affect almost every organ in the body. A report from the Royal College of Physicians estimated air pollution had contributed to 30,000 deaths in the UK in 2025 and costs the economy more than Â£27bn annually.
Holgate said communities with poorer underlying health and living conditions were more vulnerable to pollution, which he said explained why inequalities persisted even as pollution fell.
A Defra spokesperson said the government was committed to reducing harmful pollution through measures including cleaner transport, tighter emissions standards and support for local authorities.
![Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah smiles brightly at the camera. She is standing in front of rows of empty wooden chairs.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/581/cpsprodpb/c6ba/live/c0c26c50-94d8-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.jpg)
Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah developed asthma at six years old and died of an asthma attack when she was nine
Multiple clean-air policies were introduced in the period covered by the BBC's analysis between 2014 and 2024. They include cleaner buses and a shift towards lower-emission vehicles, as well as London's Ulez, which replaced the earlier Toxicity Charge (T-Charge).
Research published this year found the T-Charge and the original central London Ulez were associated with reductions in emergency hospital admissions among adults living in the zone. Another recent study found deaths linked to air pollution fell by an estimated 40% in London over five years from 2019.
Last week, a group of researchers published results from a five-year study following primary school children in London and Luton to determine if young children's lungs begin to recover under air quality improvements. Their findings show children in London whose lung growth had been stunted by pollution improved drastically in the years after the introduction of the Ulez.
A spokesperson for the Mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, said: "London's Ulez, the world's largest clean-air zone, has been a huge success in cleaning up London's air, with harmful roadside NOâ concentrations now 24% lower in outer London compared to without the Ulez in place.
"All Londoners are now breathing much cleaner air, but there is still more to do and the mayor will continue to take action as we build a greener, fairer London for everyone."
Steve McNamara, general secretary of the Licensed Taxi Drivers' Association, said cab drivers were sceptical when the Ulez was first introduced in central London in April 2019.
But he has since changed his mind.
"When you used to drive a cab around with the windows open, at the end of the day, your hand was black. You were filthy. You don't get that now. You can actually breathe the difference."
'Charging poor people is not the solution'
Despite the improvements in air quality, the expansion of the Ulez in 2023 remains controversial, with some small business owners and trade unions arguing the financial burden has fallen unfairly.
Maria Melucci, who owns an Italian deli in Bexley village in south-east London, said she had seen first hand how the expansion affected small businesses.
Many of her customers came from Kent, but many of the customers coming from outside the Ulez area now have to pay the daily Â£12.50 charge to visit her shop.
"If air pollution kills people, if it affects people's lungs, for sure we must do it," she said about the policy. "I'm not against that. But charging poor people is not the solution."
Melucci also questioned the logic behind the Ulez charge: "If that car is polluting and dangerous, then that car should be taken off the street, not pay Â£12.50 to drive anyway."
![Maria Melucci, wearing a black top, necklace and eyeliner, smiles inside her Italian deli in Bexley village. Shelves of goods and a seated customer are visible in the blurred background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/8c0e/live/7b2183e0-a147-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Maria Melucci says the Ulez expansion has affected small businesses such as her cafe and deli in Bexley village
Gavin Davies, GMB union senior organiser, said: "We are very supportive of cleaner air in London and welcome improvements to the capital's air quality, but we'd argue that more needs to be done to shield frontline workers from the costs associated with Ulez."
He said NHS workers unable to afford Ulez-compliant vehicles often could not rely on public transport for their commute during unsocial hours or to more remote sites.
He added some staff whose shifts crossed from one day into the next were being forced to pay the Ulez charge twice, creating an unfair burden on night workers.
"We'd like to see discounts to the Ulez charge applied for NHS and other frontline workers, as well as the introduction of schemes to assist them to purchase Ulez-compliant vehicles."
London has cleaned up its air faster than many expected. But while pollution has fallen across every London neighbourhood, the BBC's analysis shows communities which have historically experienced the dirtiest air continue to face higher levels of pollution.
Adoo-Kissi-Debra said she would keep pushing the government on implementing the stricter WHO air quality targets by 2030 through the proposed Clean Air (Human Rights) Bill, known as Ella's Law in memory of her daughter.
"Pollution is still there, it's just different now. Whereas 70 years ago you could see it with the naked eye, it's now hidden. You have to see it underneath a microscope," she said.
"But if people are continuing to breathe dirty air, they're going to continue to get ill."
summary: London's air quality has improved significantly over the past decade, with average nitrogen dioxide levels falling by almost 38% and every neighborhood now meeting the UK's legal limit. However, disparities persist, as deprived areas and neighborhoods with larger non-white populations still experience higher pollution levels, and fewer than 1% of London neighborhoods meet stricter World Health Organization guidelines. While clean-air initiatives like the Ultra-Low Emission Zone (Ulez) have helped reduce pollution-related illnesses and deaths, the policy's expansion and daily charges continue to draw criticism from small business owners and unions over financial burdens on low-income residents and frontline workers.
key_points: Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah became the first person in the UK to have air pollution listed on her death certificate after dying of an asthma attack linked to illegal air pollution levels in 2013.
BBC analysis shows average nitrogen dioxide levels in London have fallen by nearly 38% since 2014, and all neighborhoods now meet the UK's legal limit.
Despite overall improvements, fewer than 1% of London neighborhoods meet the World Health Organization's recommended guideline, and historically polluted areas remain the most affected.
Clean-air policies like the Ulez have been credited with improving children's lung growth and reducing emergency hospital admissions and pollution-linked deaths.
Some small business owners and union representatives argue the Ulez expansion imposes an unfair financial burden on lower-income individuals, small shops, and NHS frontline workers.

title: Yellow thunderstorm warning issued as festivalgoers face more wet weather
author: Jordan Reynolds
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/29/13/1833c5709cfa30f7190e69f84ffe701bY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg4MDkzOTYy-2.85683077.jpg?crop=8:5,smart&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
It means flooding of a few homes and businesses is likely, trains could be delayed and car journeys could take longer, the forecaster said.
Some areas within the warning could see 15-25mm of rain in an hour, and 30mm in two to three hours, along with hail and lightning.
Meanwhile, people at Reading, Leeds and other live music events are likely to see rain on Saturday as low pressure pushes eastwards, which will be followed by heavy showers.
Four areas, mainly across the Midlands, are covered by Environment Agency flood alerts, meaning floods are possible.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/29/13/992ba95f4ffef18e0da95a7f24d0755fY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg4MDkzOTk1-2.85683075.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
It comes after continued hot weather across the UK, which coincided with extremely dry conditions.
The Met Office has previously said the UK is on course for its hottest summer on record after five heatwaves, with temperatures of up to 38.1C recorded in London.
Festivalgoers at Reading Festival were pictured frolicking in the rain during the event on Friday, with many laughing and posing for photos as they remained in good spirits despite their outfits being drenched in mud.
While some were seen flinging mud at each other and playing in puddles, others were hiding beneath their plastic ponchos as they braved the poor weather conditions.
Geese frontman Cameron Winter warned festivalgoers not to “drink the water” on Friday as heavy rainfall seeped through the tent during their set.
Met Office meteorologist Greg Dewhurst said: “An area of low pressure is currently pushing eastwards across England and Wales and Northern Ireland, pushing rain across the country. That’s going to be followed by heavy showers.
“Temperatures generally reaching the low 20s, highs of 22-23C.
“It will be a different picture for Scotland even though it’s largely cloudy, there will be some brighter spells.
Read More
“For most it’s quite a bright start tomorrow, but it won’t be long before showers bubble up.
“We will see heavy showers developing throughout the day in the north and west of the UK and some thundery weather.
“With tomorrow being a bit more of a day of sunshine and showers, it should mean with a bit more sunshine around temperatures will be a bit higher, with highs of 20-23C for most and isolated areas could see 24C.
“Monday will be a brighter day for most, quite a lot of cloud around, but also showers, more frequent in the north of the UK. Temperatures may come down a touch, between 19-22C, maybe locally 23C.”
And wind gusts of 35-40mph could be seen on the south coast on Saturday, while Leeds Festival could get some gusty winds on Sunday if heavier showers hit.
summary: A yellow thunderstorm warning has been issued as low pressure brings wet weather, potential flooding, and travel disruptions following a period of hot and dry conditions. Festivalgoers at events like Reading and Leeds are facing rain, heavy showers, and muddy conditions. Meanwhile, the Environment Agency has issued flood alerts for four areas mainly across the Midlands.
key_points: A yellow thunderstorm warning brings risks of flooding, hail, lightning, and travel delays.
Festivalgoers at Reading and Leeds are experiencing heavy rain and muddy conditions.
Four areas, mainly across the Midlands, are covered by Environment Agency flood alerts.
The wet weather follows a prolonged period of hot and dry conditions, with the UK on course for its hottest summer on record.
Temperatures are generally reaching highs of 20-23C, with wind gusts expected on the south coast and potentially at Leeds Festival.

title: Pedestrian injured as bus crashes into building in London street
author: Matt Watts
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![Are the capital's bus drivers becoming more reckless? | The London Question](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/29/10/50/Bus-crash.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) The pedestrian was injured in the incident before the bus struck the building in Hayes on Friday evening. Footage shared online appears to show the H98 bus to Hounslow hit the side of the building after apparently losing control as it turned at a roundabout. The unverified clip shows the bus collide with a car and strike a man walking across the road before crashing. First Bus London said there were no passengers on board the bus when it crashed near Hayes and Harlington station at around 7.30pm. ![

The bus crashed in Hayes

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/29/10/50/Bus-crash.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) The driver suffered a minor injury and a pedestrian was also treated for minor injuries, the operator told London Bus Forum News. The company said emergency services attended the scene and that damage to the building had been confirmed as non structural, the website reported. It said the circumstances surrounding the collision would be fully investigated and that it would support the relevant authorities with their enquiries. The Standard has contacted the bus company for comment. A London Ambulance Service spokesperson said: “We were called at 7.02pm on Friday, 28 August, to reports of a road traffic collision involving a bus crashing into a building on Station Road, Hayes, UB3. “We dispatched multiple ambulance crews to the scene. We treated a male at the scene, who was later discharged.” Read More TfL said anyone affected by serious incidents on its network can contact the Sarah Hope Line for practical, financial and emotional support. It can be reached on 0343 222 5678 or at [email protected].
summary: A pedestrian and a bus driver sustained minor injuries after an empty H98 bus crashed into a building in Hayes on Friday evening. Online footage indicates the bus lost control while turning at a roundabout, hitting a car and a pedestrian before the collision. Emergency services responded to the scene, and First Bus London stated that the building's damage was confirmed as non-structural.
key_points: A pedestrian was injured after being struck by a bus in Hayes on Friday evening.
There were no passengers on board the H98 bus at the time of the crash near Hayes and Harlington station.
Both the bus driver and the pedestrian sustained minor injuries.
First Bus London confirmed the building damage was non-structural and stated that the incident will be fully investigated.

title: Cleverly quits shadow cabinet to run for London mayor
author: Adam Goldsmith
content:
![James Cleverly wears a suit and holds a microphone](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/2689/live/dc707fb0-a3be-11f1-b13c-0d78069132fa.jpg)
- Published
Conservative MP Sir James Cleverly has said he is resigning from the shadow cabinet to run for London mayor.
"I am putting myself forward to be the Conservative candidate for mayor of London, because our capital needs more than an administrator," he wrote in the Times, external.
Sir James said he has told Tory leader Kemi Badenoch he is stepping down as shadow housing secretary, saying: "I must be free to speak about every aspect of London's future and concentrate fully on winning this race."
The capital is not set to vote on a new mayor until May 2028. Labour incumbent Sir Sadiq Khan is yet to confirm whether he will seek an unprecedented fourth term.
The Conservatives are yet to pick their candidate for the London mayoral race.
A source close to Badenoch said Cleverly "is a formidable politician and will out-campaign Khan".
Sir James, who was foreign secretary under former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, wrote that he intended to make London a city to be proud of again.
"We must rebuild its reputation and make it, once again, the best place in the world to live, work, invest and build a business," he added.
A senior Conservative politician, Sir James has held a number of ministerial positions under three prime ministers - including roles as home secretary and education secretary.
The army reservist represented the Tories on the London Assembly before his election as MP for Braintree in 2015.
After rising through the backbenches, he unsuccessfully ran for Conservative party leader in 2024, losing out to Badenoch.
Reacting to Sir James's announcement, a source said Badenoch "really didn't want James to leave shadow cabinet", but believed "he will be a big asset in London".
Current London Mayor Sir Sadiq began his first term in 2016. Cleverly wrote that the capital has been "let down by Labour".
He accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of treating London as a "cash cow: somewhere to tax, regulate, raid and blame".
Sir James said: "Londoners need homes they can afford to buy or rent. Entrepreneurs need to be able to start and grow businesses without being strangled by cost and regulation."
The last time Londoners voted for their mayor in May 2024, Sir Sadiq beat Conservative rival Susan Hall by more than 275,000 votes - representing a swing of 3.2% to Labour.
The mayor won nine of the 14 constituencies including two gains from the Tories, and gained 43.8% of the vote share.
Reform UK revealed its candidate for the May 2028 election in January when it announced Westminster City councillor Laila Cunningham would be standing.
Reacting on social media, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage wrote the Conservatives are "done for", and said Cleverly "will not be the first Tory MP to give up any hope of winning their seat in Essex".
Cleverly has not resigned as an MP yet.
His announcement follows speculation in recent weeks that he would step down and launch a bid to become London's next mayor.
During his time at the London Assembly, Cleverly chaired the London Fire and Emergency Planning Authority, and also worked for Boris Johnson while he was mayor of London.
summary: Conservative MP Sir James Cleverly has resigned from the shadow cabinet as shadow housing secretary to run for the Conservative nomination for London mayor. He stated that he needs freedom to speak on London's future and concentrate on winning the race, which culminates in the May 2028 election. The Conservative Party has not yet selected its candidate for the mayoral race.
key_points: Sir James Cleverly stepped down from his role as shadow housing secretary to run for London mayor.
The next London mayoral election is scheduled for May 2028.
Cleverly has not resigned as an MP.
The Conservative Party has not yet chosen its mayoral candidate.

title: Meet the movie set: the Londoners who rent out their homes for up to £2k a day
author: Ruth Bloomfield
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Nina Watson at her Palmers Green home](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/27/16/45/Nina-Watson.jpeg?trim=157,0,158,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
![Homes & Property](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_hnp_embed_desktop.png)
When Nina Watson bought an Edwardian semi in north London she believed it would make a great home for her young family to grow up in. It has turned out to be that, and much more besides.
Buying and renovating the four-bedroom house, bought for £750,000 in 2017, set Watson on course for an accidental career change and a completely different way of life, with models posing with pythons in her living room and hundreds of thousands of social media followers raving over her signature interiors style.
Renting your home as a location for film, TV and photo shoots is becoming an increasingly popular option for homeowners looking to monetise their main asset, although Watson fell into the business quite by chance. When she and her husband Phil, who works for a local council, moved into the property with their two children, Jonah, 16, and Rosa, 14, it was “very white and beige”. The couple both love design and agreed to give it a full-on makeover.
Watson, who was working as office manager for an animation company, oversaw a slow-burn renovation of the Palmers Green house, installing period fireplaces, commissioning stained glass for the French doors, building a kitchen extension and redecorating in a style she describes as “vintage eclectic”.
She furnished the house with family heirlooms — the drinks cabinet was her grandmother’s — and online bargains including the £19.99 rich yellow three-piece suite she snapped up on eBay, the collection of 1960s Italian lighting she has picked up slowly, and the 1920s Maple & Co bed she found in an antique shop.
For fun, Watson, who hadn’t previously used social media, set up an Instagram account to chart her progress. “When we decorated the house we did it for ourselves, nobody else,” she says. Somewhat to her astonishment @artdecojewel has since picked up 650,000 followers. Then people started asking her if she could help redesign their homes.
![Nina Watson bathroom](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/27/16/16/Nina-Watson-bathroom.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
During the pandemic she was able to give up the day job and concentrate on interior design full time. Simultaneously she was contacted by The Location Guys (thelocationguys.co.uk), which represents filming locations around the country and wanted to sign her up. Naturally she jumped at the chance.
Fees range from “mates rates” of around £450 per day for student films, which Watson likes to support, up to £2,000-plus for corporate clients. The income goes on household expenses, as well as keeping the house looking perfect.
“You might get loads of bookings — we had four last week — or none”
“I wouldn’t say it is a reliable form of income,” says Watson. “You might get loads of bookings — we had four last week — or none. But my old job was a good job that was not fulfilling me creatively. And what I really enjoy is people seeing something in our property and using it as the backdrop for their own creativity.”
Weird and wonderful requests include the fashion brand which asked if they could bring a python into the house to pose with a model — Watson said yes — to the sportswear company that focused on the treehouse in the back garden, to the film-makers who installed a copper bathtub in the living room.
Unlike Watson, using her home as a location was a deliberate, strategic plan for Nicola Gill. With a large, blended family to accommodate, it was the only way she could afford a large London home.
![Nicola Gill in her Catford home](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/27/16/52/Nicola-Gill.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Gill has always loved property and while she worked as a newspaper and magazine journalist she also had a side hustle buying and renovating properties to supplement her income.
In 2014 she returned to London after a spell in Hastings, and was faced with the problem of how to afford a home spacious enough for her, her partner, Pete Wareham, a jazz musician, their four now-teenage children, and two dogs.
Some of her friends had made a success of renting their homes as locations, and Gill decided to follow suit. In 2017 she spotted a dismal five-bedroom Victorian semi for sale in Catford. “It was terrible,” she said. “It had been used as an unlicensed HMO, every single original feature had been taken out, there were toilets in the bedrooms, a terrible plastic glazed conservatory that was boiling in summer and freezing in winter. It was infested with mice and rats. It was as bad as it could be.”
Nonetheless, impressed by the square footage she could get for her money, Gill and Wareham paid £700,000 for the house and had it stripped back to bare brick. Going bold on colour was partly personal preference and partly because Gill was aware that a unique house was likely to catch the eye of location scouts. So once the structural work was done she decorated the house in blocks of vivid colour: from a coral staircase with green trim, to a cobalt blue living room, green and lilac kitchen, and orange dining room.
![Nicola Gill's coral staircase with green trim](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/27/16/54/Nicola-Gill-home.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The £200,000 renovation was slow, delayed first by a rogue builder who had to be dismissed and then by the pandemic. Nonetheless by the summer of 2022 the house was ready to show. Gill chose The Location Guys to represent her and was thrilled to get her first photoshoot booking within a week. “I had maxed out my credit cards, and I couldn’t borrow a penny more,” she said. “If it hadn’t worked I would literally have been bankrupt.”
For the first couple of years the house was in almost-constant use, booked a couple of days every week. The income, plus interior design work for clients, was enough to get her debt under control and cover the mortgage.
The past couple of years have not been quite as bountiful, which Gill blames partly on the house having become a bit overexposed in its first couple of years, and partly on the fact that brands are spending less on advertising than they once were. Bookings have slowed to four to five days per month. But with fees ranging from around £800 per day for a simple photoshoot to up to around £2,800 for a TV commercial, her mortgage is still covered.
Think your property is ready for its close-up?
Here are the essentials
● Contact an agency. Try The Location Guys (@thelocationguys), Amazing Space (amazingspace. co.uk) and Locations London (locations.london)
● You don’t need to live in a carefully curated showpiece home — normal homes are also regularly booked
● Homeowners need to keep their homes spotless because bookings are often last-minute. They also need a plan for where they will go during the shoot
● Daily fees range from around £400 to more than £2,000
● For a film or TV series the money really ramps up — £20,000-plus per month plus expenses to cover alternative accommodation
● Income is taxable, but you can claim reasonable expenses, like cleaning
But before you start studying colour charts and planning how you will spend the location windfall cash, Gill does have some words of caution. Her house has to be kept “impeccably clean” at all times — which must be a challenge with four teenagers in the home — and she also has to refresh the decor regularly to make sure it is on-trend. Although firms pay for any breakages, general wear and tear is on Gill, which means time and money has to be spent on regular maintenance too.
When the house is booked the family has to vacate, which has meant lots of long days wandering around town looking for places to hang out until the job is complete. The family’s two dogs have to go to a sitter. “It is exhausting and tiring, not money for old rope,” she said.
Not that Gill has any regrets. “We have got a house for six people in London and we don’t work in the City which is extraordinary. OK, it is in Catford, but still it is a privilege.”
summary: Renting out private homes as locations for film, television, and photo shoots has become an increasingly popular way for London homeowners to monetise their properties. Homeowners like Nina Watson and Nicola Gill renovated and uniquely decorated their houses, subsequently signing with agencies like The Location Guys to secure bookings. While daily rates can range from hundreds to thousands of pounds, the income is unpredictable, and the process requires keeping the home impeccably clean, frequent maintenance, and vacating the property during shoots.
key_points: London homeowners are renting out their properties for film, TV, and photo shoots, earning anywhere from £400 to over £2,000 per day.
Unique interior designs and bold color choices help properties stand out to location scouts and agencies like The Location Guys.
Income from location rentals is not entirely reliable, as bookings can fluctuate heavily based on trends and advertising budgets.
Participating homeowners must regularly maintain their properties, keep them spotless, and vacate the premises with their families during shoots.

title: Notting Hill Carnival: 330 people banned in massive police operation to stop violence
author: Nicholas Cecil
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Notting Hill Carnival CEO issues message to those coming to cause trouble](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/28/13/12/arrest.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
![Notting Hill Carnival 2025](https://static.standard.co.uk/2025/08/26/5/24/Notting-Hill-Carnival-2025-pj0cetbc.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
More than 7,000 officers will be deployed to west London over the August Bank Holiday in a huge Met Police operation for the carnival which is forecast to see a mixture of sun and rain on Sunday and Monday.
“Our job is to help make sure they can do that safely.”
Commander Smart added: "An event of this size inevitably brings challenges.
“Preventing serious violence, protecting women and girls and supporting the event organisers as they work to ensure crowd safety remain key areas of focus.
"We have strengthened our plans to target those who come intending to commit violence or engage in other criminality.
“We will use intelligence-led tactics including stop and search, as well as the increased deployment of live facial recognition cameras, to identify offenders, prevent harm and intervene early wherever possible.”
![A young man is handcuffed by a police officer, but after being questioned and search was released, at the Notting Hill Carnival celebration in west London over the Summer Bank Holiday weekend. Picture date: Monday August 25, 2025.](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/28/13/12/arrest.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
In pre-emptive action by the Met:
* People suspected of planning violence at the festival have been arrested and charged. Where charges were not possible, bail conditions were imposed on more than 330 people to stop them attending it.
* Scotland Yard, working with officers from Greater Manchester Police, swooped on several London addresses, arresting seven people on suspicion of robbery.
They are believed to be part of a gang that targets music events and festivals to commit serious offences.
Read More
* Raids took place to seize 66 zombie knives in north east London and 10 zombie knives, 30 flick knives and a machete in east London.
* Registered sex offenders suspected of being likely to attend the festival have had conditions attached to their licences to stop them from doing so.
* Officers visited local pubs, hotels, restaurants, fast food outlets, phone and vape shops, as well as supermarkets, to raise awareness of the risk of child sexual exploitation and trafficking.
* An order under Section 60 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 will be in place, giving officers additional search powers to find weapons.
* More live facial recognition cameras will be deployed at the event, and its approaches, after the technology identified 98 people last year leading to 61 arrests and officers stopping and speaking to 30 registered sex offenders.
“We also encourage the public to remain vigilant while travelling and to report anything that doesn't feel right.
“Speak to a police officer or member of staff, or you can text us discreetly on 61016."
At last year’s carnival, there were 528 arrests including 55 for assaulting police officers, 167 for drug offences and 50 for possession of offensive weapons, as well as four reported stabbing/slashing incidents.
summary: The Metropolitan Police launched a massive pre-emptive operation ahead of the Notting Hill Carnival, deploying over 7,000 officers and using tactics such as live facial recognition and stop-and-search powers. As part of these efforts, more than 330 individuals have been banned from attending through bail conditions or arrests to prevent violence. Police also conducted raids that seized numerous weapons, including zombie knives and machetes, and placed restrictions on registered sex offenders.
key_points: More than 7,000 officers are deployed for the west London carnival over the August Bank Holiday.
Bail conditions or arrests were used to stop more than 330 people from attending the festival.
Police raids in London led to the seizure of numerous weapons, including zombie knives and a machete.
Law enforcement is utilizing increased live facial recognition cameras and Section 60 stop-and-search powers.
Last year's event resulted in 528 arrests and four reported stabbing or slashing incidents.

title: Patti LuPone to return to London with Matters of the Heart
author: Alex Wood
content:
The Tony winner is back in London!
Three-time Tony Award winner Patti LuPone will perform her theatrical concert Matters of the Heart in London.
The engagement will mark LuPone’s return to the London Coliseum following her concert A Life in Notes, which played there in 2025. Tickets go on general sale on 4 September.
Matters of the Heart was first performed by LuPone at the Donmar Warehouse in 1999, before going on to the West End and touring nationally and internationally. The concert is based on LuPone’s 1999 recording of the same name, which was named one of the best recordings of the year by The Times and Time Out in New York.
LuPone said: “Performing my show A Life in Notes at the Coliseum in 2025 was a special night that I remember dearly. I can’t wait to come back with Matters of the Heart, which I first performed at the Donmar Warehouse in 1999. And it’s Valentine’s Day, dolls. Will you be my Valentine?”
It runs at the London Coliseum on 14 and 15 February 2027.
The concert explores the “crimes, affairs and mysteries of the heart”, with LuPone performing more than two dozen songs, spanning Broadway standards and material by contemporary songwriters.
The production is conceived and directed by Scott Wittman, with musical direction and arrangements by Joseph Thalken. The Four Play String Quartet also features in the concert.
Matters of the Heart is presented by Darren Bell Productions and Cuffe & Taylor, with general management by QUBE Theatricals.
summary: Three-time Tony Award winner Patti LuPone is returning to the London Coliseum with her theatrical concert Matters of the Heart. The engagement is scheduled for February 14 and 15, 2027, following her 2025 concert at the venue. General ticket sales begin on September 4.
key_points: Patti LuPone will perform Matters of the Heart at the London Coliseum on February 14 and 15, 2027.
Tickets go on general sale on September 4.
The concert was originally performed at the Donmar Warehouse in 1999 and is based on her recording of the same name.
The production features more than two dozen Broadway standards and contemporary songs, conceived and directed by Scott Wittman.

title: Huge fire at Neasden waste facility shuts Tube and train lines
author: James W Kelly
content:
Some 125 firefighters are tackling the blaze in north-west London
- Published
A large fire has broken out at a waste facility close to Wembley Stadium in north-west London, shutting Tube and train lines in the area.
The London Fire Brigade (LFB) said 125 firefighters were tackling the blaze at an industrial estate on Hannah Close in Neasden, with the smoke plumes visible from miles away in central London.
The LFB was alerted just after 11:30 BST and has deployed 20 fire engines to the scene. Residents have been warned to keep their windows and doors shut because of the huge amount of smoke.
Most of the Metropolitan line remains suspended due to the fire, while the Jubilee line is still part shut between Willesden Green and Wembley Park.
The fire had suspended the entire Metropolitan line for several hours on Friday afternoon. It has partially reopened but remains suspended between Harrow-on-the-Hill and Aldgate, meaning no services are running in central London.
Rail services to and from London Marylebone are also being delayed or cancelled due to train lines to Aylesbury being affected, National Rail said.
Disruption is set to last well into the Friday evening.
![An aerial view of a large industrial warehouse unit with smoke billowing from its roof, while a London Fire Brigade turntable ladder directs water onto the building from below.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1040/cpsprodpb/dcf8/live/f879c460-a2eb-11f1-a789-b16da4059b6b.jpg)
The industrial unit on fire measures approximately 100m by 150m (161,400 sq ft), according to the LFB
Speaking from the scene, LFB Assistant Commissioner Andy Pennick said firefighters were met by a well-developed fire involving a waste transfer facility and immediately requested 20 fire engines.
"This is a protracted incident that will see crews on scene for the remainder of the day as the work to fully extinguish the fire," he said.
"I'd like to thank our firefighters for their hard work so far at this fire, and our control officers for managing a significant number of calls and coordinating or response."
![A thick plume of dark grey smoke rises into the sky behind a modern multi-storey building, overhead line gantries, and a arched railway bridge.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/f17b/live/005d0630-a2db-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
TfL suspended the Metropolitan line and part of the Jubilee line due to the proximity of the blaze
A TfL spokesperson said: "We're continuing to liaise with LFB to make sure we understand what we can operate safely for both our customers and staff."
The industrial unit on fire measures approximately 100m by 150m (161,400 sq ft), the LFB said.
The facility is run by London Energy, a company owned by the North London Waste Authority, which is responsible for disposing all waste for the boroughs of Barnet, Camden, Enfield, Hackney, Haringey, Islington and Waltham Forest.
A spokesperson for the firm said: "We are currently responding to a fire at our Wembley transfer station and are working closely with the emergency services and relevant authorities.
"We can confirm that all London Energy employees are safe and there have been no injuries."
![People gather outside the closed metal shutters of Neasden Station entrance, with one man gesturing towards the station signs while commuters wait on the pavement.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/f7c4/live/37e9d950-a2ec-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Travel disruption is set to run into Friday evening's rush hour
The LFB said it had received more than 70 calls reporting the blaze, and its cause is unknown.
BBC News understands that an Amazon delivery facility based in the industrial estate has not been directly impacted by the fire, but staff have been evacuated as precaution.

summary: A large fire broke out at a waste facility in Neasden, north-west London, prompting a response from 125 firefighters and 20 fire engines. The blaze caused significant disruption to local transport, suspending parts of the Metropolitan and Jubilee Tube lines and affecting rail services to and from London Marylebone. Residents were advised to keep their windows and doors closed due to heavy smoke, and travel disruptions are expected to continue into the evening.
key_points: Around 125 firefighters and 20 fire engines tackled the blaze at an industrial estate on Hannah Close.
The fire caused major travel disruptions, suspending parts of the Metropolitan and Jubilee lines and delaying rail services to London Marylebone.
Residents in the area were warned to keep windows and doors shut due to heavy smoke visible from central London.
All London Energy employees were confirmed safe with no injuries reported, and an adjacent Amazon facility evacuated staff as a precaution.
The cause of the fire remains unknown, and crews are expected to remain at the scene for the remainder of the day.

title: Residents board up their properties ahead of Notting Hill Carnival
author: Niva Yadav
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Metal fences and wooden barricades have been fitted on houses and shopfronts in west London as the 60th edition of Notting Hill Carnival approaches](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/27/15/58/Screenshot-2026-08-27-at-16-31-46.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Locals have previously voiced complaints about noise, litter, and even revellers defecating or fornicating in front gardens.
Last year, 55 complaints were filed to the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelse, comprising issues of noise, disturbance, and environmental health.
Such behaviour has prompted dozens to board up their homes in anticipation.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/27/15/59/Screenshot-2026-08-27-at-16-31-58.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
“Every year we have to deal with people being sick in our garden or leaving their rubbish,” she said.
“It’s not really fair.”
She added that while she “loves carnival and what it does for the community,” she was “sick and tired” of “the mess and noise.”
“It keeps the kids safe,” she explained.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/27/15/15/Screenshot-2026-08-27-at-16-35-50.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/27/15/41/Screenshot-2026-08-27-at-16-31-30.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Local businesses have also erected plywood boards as the streets prepare for the festivities.
Both Tesco Express and Sainsbury’s Local on Portobello Road and Ladbroke Grove respectively have boarded up their shopfronts as they prepare for the festivities.
Read More
Both shops are expected to stay open.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/27/15/45/Screenshot-2026-08-27-at-16-30-40.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
In the heart of Portobello Market, one trader said that while the carnival “brings good customers”, it is “too busy and stressful” for small businesses.
He said it was easier to board up the shop “for peace of mind”.
But others have suggested that it is merely a small tribulation of living in Notting Hill and residents in the area should expect noise and litter - or live elsewhere.
It’s similar to the argument put forward by critics of the Soho Society in Westminster, after complaints were made about late night licensing.
“If you’re living in Notting Hill, then it’s just part of the package, part of the culture,” said one man.
He said he had lived in the area for over 20 years and urged people “to live somewhere else” if Carnival posed such a problem.
“Get involved!,” he said.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/27/15/21/Screenshot-2026-08-27-at-16-31-05.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Last year, there were no noise limits set for the festivities, but it is understood that this year, limits have been set and will be monitored by the council.
As per Carnival rules, sound systems and mas bands must wind down the noise by 7pm.
In 2025, no equipment was seized or confiscated as a result of breaches of curfew time or non-compliance.
summary: Residents and local businesses in west London are boarding up their properties with metal fences and wooden barricades ahead of the 60th Notting Hill Carnival. The preparations follow previous complaints regarding noise, litter, and anti-social behaviour from revellers during the event. While many locals view the boarding as a necessary protection for peace of mind, some residents argue that such disruptions are simply part of living in the area.
key_points: Locals and shopfronts, including Tesco Express and Sainsbury's Local, have fitted wooden and metal barricades ahead of the Notting Hill Carnival.
Precautions are driven by past issues with noise, litter, and anti-social behavior from revellers in front gardens.
Last year, the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea received 55 complaints regarding noise, disturbances, and environmental health.
Some long-term residents believe that dealing with the noise and mess is part of living in Notting Hill culture.
Sound systems and mas bands are required to lower noise levels by 7pm under council rules.

title: 'Nanny McPhee' world premiere to open in London in 2027 | London Theatre
author: Olivia Rook
content:
![](https://images.ctfassets.net/6pezt69ih962/359kig96gYHyY4rDRseDEa/b16ca9ca23131192fc824bfb5acb441c/download.jpg?h=200&fm=webp&q=90)
![A person with short blond hair, red lipstick, and a light blue collared shirt smiles while standing against a beige textured wall.](https://images.ctfassets.net/6pezt69ih962/LMWH2Kh60ai0O0DmWMQAz/c620225f5bae99afb62cea715d765e23/Emma_Thompson_1200_LT_Photo_by_Nick_Haddow.jpg?h=550&fm=webp&q=90)
'Nanny McPhee' world premiere to open in London in 2027
Joining Academy Award, BAFTA, Golden Globe and Emmy Award-winning actor and writer Emma Thompson in the creative team of the Nanny McPhee musical is singer-songwriter Gary Clark, who provides the music, with original lyrics by Emma Thompson and Gary Clark.
Summary
- A Nanny McPhee musical is coming to the London stage
- Performances will begin in summer 2027
- Emma Thompson has provided the book and original lyrics
![Olivia Rook](https://images.ctfassets.net/6pezt69ih962/2AnVizCwXsbKHoScEZBHKl/7b2e062e88ede030d9eea0db2bb6a632/Author_bio_pic_for_website.jpg?w=32&h=32)
A new musical stage adaptation of Nanny McPhee, with a book by Academy Award winner Emma Thompson, will open in London in summer 2027.
Based on the Nanny McPhee films, and the Nurse Matilda character by Christianna Brand and Edward Ardizzone that inspired them, the new musical will follow the mysterious figure of Nanny McPhee, as she arrives at the Browns’ door and discovers a household in chaos. As she begins to restore harmony, we learn that adults, as well as the children, have lessons to learn.
The original 2005 film, written by and starring Emma Thompson in the title role, also featured Colin Firth, Angela Lansbury, Kelly Macdonald, Imelda Staunton and Thomas Brodie-Sangster. Thompson also wrote and starred in the 2010 sequel Nanny McPhee and the Big Bang.
Joining Academy Award, BAFTA, Golden Globe and Emmy Award-winning actor and writer Emma Thompson in the creative team is singer-songwriter Gary Clark, who provides the music, with original lyrics by Emma Thompson and Gary Clark. Katy Rudd (Ballet Shoes and The Ocean at the End of the Lane), will direct, with set and costume designs by Tony and Olivier Award winner Rob Howell (Matilda the Musical) and choreography by Ellen Kane.
Emma Thompson said: "I’ve lived with Nanny McPhee for so long that to see her finally tread the boards is supremely exciting. Theatre feels like her natural home - magic, music, mischief and a good dollop of danger can all happen right in front of you. Working with Gary Clark to create the musical heart that beats through the story has been an unforgettable journey of a lifetime. And I am thrilled and so proud that the brilliant Katy Rudd will be bringing it all to life with her inimitable witty wonderment. I can't wait to introduce the all-new Nanny McPhee to audiences next summer.”
The award-winning creative team also includes orchestrations by Simon Hale, music supervision by Nigel Lilley, music arrangements by Simon Hale and Nigel Lilley, lighting by Howard Hudson, sound design by Ian Dickinson for Autograph, illusions by Chris Fisher, puppetry by Samuel Wyer, and projections by Andrzej Goulding.
Further information, including the theatre, performance dates and casting are yet to be announced.

title: London Fire Brigade tackles Mitcham industrial site fire
author: Amy Clarke
content:
![Firefighters stand beside a London Fire Brigade engine as thick black smoke rises from a large fire behind nearby buildings in Mitcham. Emergency crews have cordoned off the area while tackling the blaze at a workshop and scaffolding yard.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/4901/live/f08d4900-a176-11f1-87d4-e91caee13898.jpg)
Twenty fire engines were called to the blaze in Mitcham
- Published
Fire crews will continue to work overnight to fully extinguish a large fire which broke out at an industrial site in south London, sending thick black smoke across the area.
The premises contain a workshop, tyre centre and scaffolding yard. The fire spread to about eight hectares (nearly 20 acres) of surrounding scrubland, as well as part of a house.
The London Fire Brigade (LFB) sent about 125 firefighters and 20 fire engines to the scene near Carshalton Road in Mitcham.
The cause of the fire is not yet known and there are currently no reports of any injuries. Multiple hotspots remain alight, but the fire was declared under control by the LFB at 20:28 BST.
![Smoke from large fire above a yellow field, with trees on the horizon.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/a9f2/live/ed0137e0-a17d-11f1-9619-edac4fa7937f.jpg)
The fire spread to scrubland around the industrial estate
More than 70 emergency calls were received by the control room from about 16:30 BST, and personnel from Mitcham, Wallington and Norbury stations were sent to the scene.
Passengers hoping to travel through Mitcham Junction should check the status of their trains as the railway remains affected by the fire and some services have been cancelled.
Road closures have also been put in place on London Road and Carshalton Road at the junctions of Willow Lane, Goat Road and Hackbridge Road.
Station Commander Jim Berry, who attended the scene, said: "Firefighters have worked hard this evening and have now brought this fire in Mitcham under control.
"Firefighting operations will continue overnight as crews fully extinguish the fire and dampen down hotspots, so please continue to avoid the area if you can."
